introduction_markdown: CAMEROON GENERAL CERTIFICATE OF EDUCATION BOARD, General Certificate of Education Examination. 0785 Religious Studies 1, JUNE 2019, ADVANCED LEVEL. Multiple choice question paper, one and a half hours. Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room. Instructions to candidates: use a soft HB pencil throughout the examination; do not open the booklet until told to do so; check that the booklet is headed 'Advanced Level - 0785 Religious Studies 1'; fill in the information required on the answer sheet (Candidate Name, Exam Session, Subject Code and Candidate Identification Number). Answer ALL the 50 questions in this Examination. All questions carry equal marks. Each question has FOUR suggested answers: A, B, C and D. Decide which answer is appropriate, find the number of the question on the answer sheet and draw a horizontal line across the letter to join the square brackets for the answer you have chosen. Mark only one answer for each question: if you mark more than one answer you will score a zero for that question. Avoid spending too much time on any one question; you can come back to it later. Do all rough work in the booklet using the blank spaces. At the end of the examination the invigilator collects the answer sheet first and then the question booklet.

questions.enonce_markdown: Abram and his family made their first stopover from UR at:
questions.corrige_markdown: Genesis 11 tells how Terah took Abram, Sarai and Lot out of Ur of the Chaldeans to go to Canaan, but the family stopped and settled at Haran. Oaks of Mamre, Bethel and Shechem are places Abram reached only later, once he had entered Canaan (Genesis 12 and 13). **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel

questions.enonce_markdown: Abraham's lie in Egypt had a deeper significance which was:
questions.corrige_markdown: In Genesis 12 Abraham presents Sarah as his sister during a famine in Egypt. His stated fear was for his own life, but the deeper significance in the narrative is that God's promise of a great nation, which depended on Sarah as the future mother of the heir, was at risk; God's intervention against Pharaoh's household shows him preserving the promise. Political power is never Abraham's aim, and 'protecting his wife' is only the surface reading, since he actually exposed her to danger. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel

questions.enonce_markdown:
An event which made Abraham unique as the father of faith is:

*Options as printed:* A) The covenant with God   B) The rescue of Lot, his nephew   C) The birth of Isaac   D) The sacrifice of Isaac
questions.corrige_markdown:
Abraham is called the father of faith above all because of the test of Genesis 22, where he obeyed God's command and was ready to offer Isaac, the child of the promise, trusting that God would keep his word. The biblical tradition (for example Hebrews 11) singles out this obedience as the model of faith. The covenant of Genesis 15 and 17 is also a key event, which is why this printed question is left open rather than auto-marked; the rescue of Lot and the birth of Isaac do not by themselves express his faith in this way.

**Intended answer: D (The sacrifice of Isaac).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel

questions.enonce_markdown: What outstanding lesson can we learn from the story of Joseph?
questions.corrige_markdown: The Joseph story (Genesis 37 to 50) shows that wrongdoing has consequences: the brothers' jealousy and deceit towards Joseph and Jacob leave them in guilt and fear, while Joseph's integrity is finally vindicated. Joseph himself says in Genesis 50 that God turned what was meant for evil into good. The other options contradict the biblical message: God is aware of human weakness, does not favour deceivers, and does not dislike the righteous. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel

choix.texte: God takes no records of human weaknesses
God does not like the just

questions.enonce_markdown: Joseph is considered as an upright man because he:
questions.corrige_markdown: In Genesis 39 Joseph refuses the advances of Potiphar's wife, saying that he could not do such a wicked thing and sin against God. This moral integrity, not his looks, his office or his dreams, is what marks him as upright. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel

choix.texte: Was in charge of the distribution of food

questions.enonce_markdown: It is one of the major themes in the story of Joseph:
questions.corrige_markdown: The story climaxes in Genesis 45 and 50, where Joseph forgives the brothers who sold him and provides for them and their families. Forgiveness and reconciliation are therefore a major theme; prudence, endurance and hard work appear in the story but are not its central message. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel

questions.enonce_markdown: Who led the Israelites into the Promised Land?
questions.corrige_markdown: Moses died before the crossing of the Jordan; according to the Book of Joshua, God appointed Joshua as his successor and Joshua led the people into Canaan. Aaron was Moses' brother and priest, and Hur is known as one of those who supported Moses' hands in battle. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - exodus and moses

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which feast marked the beginning of the Exodus?

*Options as printed:* A) The Pesach   B) The Passover   C) Tabernacle   D) Yom kippur
questions.corrige_markdown:
Exodus 12 describes the Passover meal on the night before the Israelites left Egypt, and the feast commemorates that deliverance. Pesach is the Hebrew name of the Passover, so options A and B name the same feast; this is why the printed question is left open. The Feast of Tabernacles recalls the wilderness journey and Yom Kippur is the Day of Atonement.

**Intended answer: B (The Passover).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - exodus and moses

questions.enonce_markdown: Where did the Israelite elders summon Samuel to demand for a king?
questions.corrige_markdown: In 1 Samuel 8 the elders of Israel gathered and came to Samuel at Ramah, his home and the place of his judgeship, asking him to appoint a king to judge them like the other nations. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judges and the monarchy

questions.enonce_markdown: The first incident which destroyed the relationship between Samuel and Saul was:
questions.corrige_markdown: The first break comes in 1 Samuel 13 at Gilgal: Saul, impatient at Samuel's delay, offered the burnt offering himself, which was a priestly act, and Samuel told him that his kingdom would not endure. The sparing of Agag and of the best of the Amalekite spoil (options B and C, which describe the same episode) happened later, in 1 Samuel 15. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judges and the monarchy

questions.enonce_markdown:
There was none like him throughout Israel in terms of achievements:

*Options as printed:* A) Samuel   B) Saul   C) Solomon   D) David
questions.corrige_markdown:
Solomon is the king remembered for unmatched wisdom, wealth and building achievements, above all the Temple (1 Kings 3 to 10). Another reading could point to David, which is why the printed question is left open for self-assessment.

**Intended answer: C (Solomon).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judges and the monarchy

questions.enonce_markdown: David's son who hatched a conspiracy against him was:
questions.corrige_markdown: Absalom, David's son, won the hearts of the people and had himself proclaimed king at Hebron, forcing David to flee Jerusalem (2 Samuel 15). Solomon was the son who later succeeded David; Abimelech was a son of Gideon in the period of the Judges. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judges and the monarchy

questions.enonce_markdown: David committed the sin of adultery with:
questions.corrige_markdown: 2 Samuel 11 recounts David's adultery with Bathsheba, wife of Uriah the Hittite, followed by the arrangement of Uriah's death. Rachel and Leah were Jacob's wives and Zilpah was Leah's maid. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judges and the monarchy

questions.enonce_markdown: He was the king in Israel when the worship of Baal was at its apex:
questions.corrige_markdown: Ahab, married to the Phoenician princess Jezebel, built a temple and altar for Baal in Samaria and promoted Baal worship; this is the background of Elijah's contest on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 16 to 18). Josiah, by contrast, was a reforming king who removed such cults. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - prophets of israel and judah

questions.enonce_markdown:
How was Israel at the time of prophet Jeremiah?

*Options as printed:* A) Overtaken by violence   B) Had become a nation of Idolaters   C) The Glory of the Lord left the Temple   D) She was actually corrupt
questions.corrige_markdown:
Jeremiah's preaching, for example in Jeremiah 2 and 7, accuses Judah of abandoning the Lord for other gods, that is idolatry, and of social corruption and injustice. Options B and D both describe the people as presented by Jeremiah, so the printed question is left open. The departure of the Lord's glory from the Temple is a theme of Ezekiel rather than Jeremiah.

**Intended answer: B (Had become a nation of Idolaters).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - prophets of israel and judah

questions.enonce_markdown: As a prophet Amos' interest was centered on:
questions.corrige_markdown: Amos, a prophet of the eighth century BCE, is known as the prophet of social justice: he denounces those who oppress the poor and sell the needy and calls for justice to roll down like waters (Amos 5). His concern is therefore God as defender of the rights of the poor. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - prophets of israel and judah

choix.texte: God will punish those who forsake him
The North will be reunited with the South
God is the defender of the rights of the poor

questions.enonce_markdown: The three Jewels of Buddhism are:
questions.corrige_markdown: The Three Jewels (also called the Triple Gem) are the Buddha, the Dhamma (his teaching) and the Sangha (the community), in which Buddhists take refuge. Options B and C are items from the moral precepts, not the Three Jewels. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - buddhism

choix.texte: I take refuge in Buddha, Dhama, Sangha
I refrain from lying, wrong speech, killing
I avoid using Jewellery, perfumes, dancing
I take refuge in meditation, reading, prayers

questions.enonce_markdown: The cycle of birth, suffering, death and rebirth is called:
questions.corrige_markdown: Samsara is the cycle of birth, suffering, death and rebirth from which Buddhists seek release. The Sangha is the community, stupas are monuments, and Soka Gakkai is a modern Buddhist movement. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - buddhism

questions.enonce_markdown: The main text of Mahayana Buddhism is written in:
questions.corrige_markdown: Many of the main Mahayana scriptures (the sutras) were composed or preserved in Sanskrit, whereas the Tipitaka is the Pali Canon of the Theravada school, and is a collection of texts rather than a language. Sangha is the community and Kisa Gotami is a figure in a well-known story of the Buddha's teaching. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - buddhism

questions.enonce_markdown: There are two main groups of scriptures in the Hindu tradition called:
questions.corrige_markdown: Hindu scriptures are classified as Shruti ('what is heard', the revealed texts such as the Vedas and Upanishads) and Smriti ('what is remembered', including the epics and the Puranas). The Mahabharata and Ramayana are examples of Smriti, and Atman and Brahman are concepts, not groups of texts. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - hinduism

questions.enonce_markdown: In Hinduism, 'Brahman' is real and everything else is 'maya' meaning:
questions.corrige_markdown: In the Vedanta tradition Brahman is the ultimate, unchanging reality, while the world of appearances is called maya, understood as illusion or having no lasting reality. 'Eternal and unchanging' describes Brahman, not maya. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - hinduism

questions.enonce_markdown: It is a process of a series of births and rebirths:
questions.corrige_markdown: Samsara is the cycle of repeated births and rebirths. Moksha is liberation from that cycle, and karma is the law of action and consequence that shapes it. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - hinduism

questions.enonce_markdown: The flight of the prophet Muhammad from Mecca to Medina took place in the year:
questions.corrige_markdown: The Hijra, the migration of Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Medina, took place in 622 CE and marks the start of the Islamic calendar. Muslims commonly date the Prophet's birth to about 570 CE and his death to 632 CE. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - life of prophet muhammad

questions.enonce_markdown: The birth place of Islam was:
questions.corrige_markdown: According to Islamic tradition the first revelations came to Muhammad in Mecca, which is therefore regarded as the birthplace of Islam. Medina was the city of the Hijra, where the first Muslim community was organised. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - life of prophet muhammad

questions.enonce_markdown: Mohammad's call came to him when he was:
questions.corrige_markdown: According to Islamic tradition Muhammad received the first revelation at about the age of forty, in the cave of Hira near Mecca. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - life of prophet muhammad

questions.enonce_markdown: Charity in Islam is expressed through:
questions.corrige_markdown: Zakat, the obligatory almsgiving, is the pillar through which charity is expressed. Hajj is pilgrimage, Sawm is fasting and Salat is prayer. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - five pillars of islam

questions.enonce_markdown: A collection of stories and sayings from the life of Muhammad (SAS) are contained in the:
questions.corrige_markdown: The Hadith are the reports of the sayings and actions of the Prophet. The Qur'an is the revealed scripture, the Injil is the Gospel as named in the Qur'an, and a surah is a chapter of the Qur'an. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - islamic scriptures and law

questions.enonce_markdown: What is the meaning of the 'Qibla' in Islam?
questions.corrige_markdown: The Qibla is the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca, towards which Muslims turn in prayer; in a mosque it is shown by the mihrab. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - islamic worship and practices

choix.texte: Indicates the position of the moon

questions.enonce_markdown: He is the spiritual leader in all Muslim communities:
questions.corrige_markdown: The Imam leads the congregation in prayer and gives spiritual guidance in the community. The muezzin and the mu'adhin are the same office, the person who gives the call to prayer, and a mualim is a teacher. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - islamic community and leadership

questions.enonce_markdown: The universal community of Muslim believers is called:
questions.corrige_markdown: The Ummah is the worldwide community of Muslims. A mumin is an individual believer, Makkah is Mecca and Jumu'ah is the Friday prayer. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - islamic community and leadership

questions.enonce_markdown:
The brain behind the Hadiths is:

*Options as printed:* A) Muhammad   B) Abu Bakr   C) Umar   D) Ali
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Hadith are the reports of the words and deeds of the Prophet Muhammad, so he is their source; the later work of collecting and verifying them was done by scholars. The wording 'brain behind' is vague, since it could also be read as asking who initiated their compilation, which is why the printed question is left open.

**Intended answer: A (Muhammad).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - islamic scriptures and law

questions.enonce_markdown: That which is forbidden according to the Islamic law is:
questions.corrige_markdown: Haram designates what is forbidden in Islamic law, in contrast with halal, what is permitted. A mihrab is the prayer niche in a mosque and zuhd is asceticism. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - islamic scriptures and law

questions.enonce_markdown: How do Muslims refer to Friday congregational prayers?
questions.corrige_markdown: The Friday congregational prayer is called Jumu'ah. Eid al-Fitr is the festival ending Ramadan and Asr is the afternoon prayer. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - islamic worship and practices

questions.enonce_markdown: The purification ritual in Islam before prayers is called:
questions.corrige_markdown: Wudu is the ritual washing performed before prayer. A rak'ah is a unit of the prayer and the mu'adhin is the person who calls to prayer. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - islamic worship and practices

questions.enonce_markdown: In which town did prophet Muhammad make a stopover during the Miraj?
questions.corrige_markdown: Islamic tradition, based on Surah 17 (al-Isra), holds that the Prophet was taken in a night journey from Mecca to the farthest mosque, identified with Jerusalem, from where he ascended through the heavens (the Miraj). Jerusalem is therefore the stopover. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - life of prophet muhammad

questions.enonce_markdown: The two major groupings in Islam are known as:
questions.corrige_markdown: The two main branches of Islam are the Sunni, the large majority, and the Shia. Wahhabism is a reform movement within Sunni Islam and Mujahideen is a general term, not a branch. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - islamic community and leadership

questions.enonce_markdown: The first pillar of Islam is:
questions.corrige_markdown: The five pillars in their usual order are Shahada (the declaration of faith), Salat (prayer), Zakat (almsgiving), Sawm (fasting in Ramadan) and Hajj (pilgrimage). The first is the Shahada. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - five pillars of islam

questions.enonce_markdown:
An important part of the Jewish Scripture is:

*Options as printed:* A) Nevi'im   B) Mishnah   C) Torah   D) Tenakh
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Torah, the five books of Moses, is the central and most revered part of the Jewish scriptures. The Nevi'im (the Prophets) are also a part of the Tanakh, and the Tanakh is the whole Hebrew Bible rather than a part, which is why the printed question is left open. The Mishnah is a later collection of rabbinic oral teaching.

**Intended answer: C (Torah).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judaism

questions.enonce_markdown: The thoughts and interpretation of the Rabbis are found in the:
questions.corrige_markdown: The Talmud brings together the Mishnah (the written record of rabbinic oral law) and the Gemara (the later rabbinic discussion of it), and is the main collection of the rabbis' thought and interpretation. The Torah is the written scripture itself. The Mishnah and the Gemara are each a component of the Talmud, so the Talmud is the best answer. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judaism

questions.enonce_markdown:
To which event can you trace the beginning of Judaism:

*Options as printed:* A) The call of Abraham   B) The Exodus of the Israelites   C) The birth of Moses   D) The Passover
questions.corrige_markdown:
Jewish tradition traces the beginning of the faith to God's call of Abraham and the covenant with him (Genesis 12 and 17), from which the people of Israel descend. The Exodus and the giving of the Law through Moses are, however, also presented as the founding of the nation, so the printed question is left open.

**Intended answer: A (The call of Abraham).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judaism
